rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer:
You pick the order; timestamps don't matter. You can get 6 counters by applying Hardened Scales first, or 5 by applying Doubling Season first. Choose Scales first for 6.

**Walking Ballista** says "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it." With X=2, that is a replacement effect (`614.1c`). Both of your effects apply to it. The Hardened Scales ruling says a creature entering with counters gets the extra one, and the Doubling Season ruling says it affects permanents that enter with counters. When several replacement effects modify the same event, the affected object's controller chooses the order (`616.1`). None of the special-priority steps apply, so any applicable effect may be chosen (`616.1e`). Each effect applies only once (`614.5`).

- Scales first: 2+1 = 3, then doubled = **6**.
- Doubling Season first: 2×2 = 4, then +1 = **5**.
citations: rule 614.1c: "Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,” “As [this permanent] enters . . . ,” or “[This permanent] enters as . . . “ are replacement effects."
rule 616.1: "the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply"
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."
rule 614.5: "A replacement effect doesn’t invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event."
ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/86e5ac2af77f77bf: "If a creature you control would enter the battlefield with a number of +1/+1 counters on it, it enters with that many plus one instead."
ruling 01546b7d-a233-4176-8843-d732074dc5b6/30e1af27509ea83b: "Doubling Season affects permanents that enter with counters."
oracle 4b515bb0-f275-4400-8032-3173b799ab40#0: "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it."

rows.question: opp cast [[Blood Moon]] while i have all three tron lands out. do i still get my 7 mana from urza's? can i tap tower for 3 colorless or is it just a Mountain now
rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer:
No. Under **Blood Moon** each Tron land is just a Mountain that taps for {R}. Three lands make three red mana, not 7 mana. **Urza's Tower** can't tap for {C}{C}{C}.

Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That is a type-changing effect, applied in layer 4 (`613.1d`). Under `305.7`, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type." So the Tower, Mine and Power Plant lose their {C} abilities and their Urza's land types. The Urza's lands' bonus only checks for those land types, so it wouldn't work even if the text stayed. Each land keeps only "{T}: Add {R}." This applies immediately, so you can't tap for the full amount in response once Blood Moon has resolved. You can tap them in response to the spell while it is still on the stack.
citations: oracle 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae#0: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."

rule 305.7: "It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type."
rule 613.1d: "Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied."
ruling 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae/de7b24c7cfc8d0d2: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had."

rows.question: follow up: what if I play [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]] AFTER the moon is already down? urborg has the later timestamp so shouldn't it make everything a Swamp too? my friend says no
rows.expected_answer: Your friend is right. Both effects are layer 4 type-changing effects (613.1d). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's (613.8a): applying Blood Moon makes Urborg a Mountain and strips its rules-text ability (305.7), which removes the existence of Urborg's effect. When a dependency exists it overrides timestamps (613.8), so Blood Moon applies first no matter which entered later (613.8b). Urborg is just a Mountain with '{T}: Add {R}' and nothing becomes a Swamp. (Any actual basic Swamps you control are still Swamps because Blood Moon only affects nonbasic lands.)

outcome.answer:
Your friend is right. If a Blood Moon-style effect (like Magus of the Moon) is on the battlefield, Urborg doesn't turn lands into Swamps, whichever came first. Timestamp doesn't decide this.

Blood Moon-style effects set nonbasic lands to be Mountains, not in addition to their other types. Per 305.7, that land "loses all abilities generated from its rules text", and Urborg's is one of those abilities. The Scryfall ruling says: "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."

Dependency explains why the later timestamp doesn't matter. Both effects apply in layer 4, and Urborg's effect depends on the moon's effect. Per 613.8a, an effect depends on another if applying the other "would change the text or the existence of the first effect". Per 613.8b, a dependent effect "waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied". Dependency overrides the timestamp system (613.8). So the moon effect applies first, Urborg loses its ability, and nothing becomes a Swamp. Urborg itself is just a Mountain with no abilities.
citations: ruling db6174d7-211d-4817-b8e4-8384594c83f9/aebb4d57471c5c28: "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."
rule 305.7: "It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land"
rule 613.8a: "applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect"
rule 613.8b: "An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied."

rows.question: my goyf has two +1/+1 counters on it and I just giant growthed it. opponent [[Clone]]s it. is their clone a huge goyf too or just a regular one? and does the clone even know how big a goyf should be since the p/t is */*+1
rows.expected_answer: Just a regular Tarmogoyf. A copy acquires only the copiable values of the original (707.2): name, mana cost, types, rules text, printed P/T, etc. Counters, Giant Growth's +3/+3, and other non-copy effects are not copiable values, so the Clone gets none of them. The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, and therefore its characteristic-defining ability (707.2a), so the Clone's own P/T is */*+1 computed from card types in graveyards (applied in layer 7a, 613.4a). The copy effect itself is applied in layer 1a (613.2a); your goyf's counters and pump are layer 7c (613.4c) and stay on your goyf only.

outcome.answer:
The Clone is just a regular Goyf. It copies neither the counters nor the Giant Growth boost. It also doesn't need to "know" a size, because the */*+1 is calculated live from the graveyards.

Copying uses only copiable values, the printed text as modified by other copy effects. Per 707.2, "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied." Your two +1/+1 counters and Giant Growth's +3/+3 stay on your Tarmogoyf only. The Scryfall Clone ruling says the same: it doesn't copy "any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness, types, color, or so on."

The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, so it gets the ability "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1." That ability works in all zones. The Clone's P/T is therefore N/N+1, where N is the number of card types among cards in all graveyards. Giant Growth is in the graveyard once it resolves, so it already counts as an instant.

Your Goyf is that same N/N+1 with two +1/+1 counters and +3/+3 on top, so it's 5 points of power and toughness larger than the Clone.
citations: rule 707.2: "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied."
rule 707.2a: "A copy acquires the abilities of the object it’s copying because those values are derived from its rules text."
ruling 42226b87-0746-4ebf-9fd0-108d508462af/e115f2763b5d5e7e: "It doesn't copy whether that creature is tapped or untapped, whether it has any counters on it or Auras and Equipment attached to it"
ruling 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd/85558f17a09ae6e1: "The ability that defines Tarmogoyf's power and toughness works in all zones, not just the battlefield."
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every ordinary creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment. Any other non-Aura enchantment Opalescence animates follows Humility itself: its base power and toughness are its mana value when Opalescence is later, and 1/1 when Humility is.

outcome.answer:
If Humility was out first, Humility becomes a 4/4 enchantment creature with no abilities, and your other creatures stay 1/1. If Opalescence was out first, Humility is a 1/1 instead, and all creatures are 1/1. In both cases Humility's effect keeps working.

**Humility first, then Opalescence.** Walk the layers:
- Layer 4: Opalescence makes Humility a creature. It doesn't animate itself, so Opalescence stays a plain enchantment.
- Layer 6: Humility strips abilities from all creatures, including itself.
- Layer 7b: both effects set base P/T. Humility's is 1/1 and Opalescence's is 4/4 (Humility's mana value). Within a sublayer, the earlier timestamp applies first (`613.7`), and Humility's is earlier. Opalescence's 4/4 is applied last, so it wins.

Humility keeps applying even though it has lost its own ability. Once an effect starts applying, it keeps applying in later layers (`613.6`).

**Opalescence first, then Humility.** Humility now has the later timestamp, so its 1/1 applies last. Humility is a 1/1 creature.

The official ruling for this interaction matches both orderings.
citations: rule 613.6: "If an effect starts to apply in one layer and/or sublayer, it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer and/or sublayer, even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process."
rule 613.4b: "Effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied."
rule 613.7: "An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp."
ruling ed7bdb3e-5c51-4547-9266-76a791e0b2b0/18649cad787b2eba: "But if Humility entered before Opalescence, the following is true:"
oracle 59489b46-9d02-4f3c-bcd0-884e7605e9a5#0: "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types"

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes to the first part, no to the second. **Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** is a modal double-faced card. You choose which face to cast before it goes on the stack (`712.11b`), so you can cast Tibalt for {5}{B}{R}, which is 7 mana. Only the face you cast is checked for whether it can be cast (`712.11c`). Once it's on the stack or battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that's up (`712.8f`).

In your library or graveyard, it has only its front-face characteristics (`712.8a`). That makes it a creature card (Valki), not a planeswalker card. In those zones it doesn't count as a planeswalker for anything.

With your two cards: **Vraska's Contempt** says "Exile target creature or planeswalker." It hits Tibalt only while he's a planeswalker on the battlefield (`712.8f`). **Kaya's Ghostform** can enchant Tibalt, because he's a planeswalker you control. When he dies or is exiled, it returns "that card" to the battlefield. A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from another zone enters front face up by default (`712.14`). So he comes back as Valki, the creature, and not as Tibalt. Valki's enters trigger then happens again.
citations: rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.11c: "Only the face that will be face up on the stack is evaluated to determine if it can be cast."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
rule 712.14: "A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters the battlefield with its front face up by default."
oracle 38ddbe0b-07ef-4cdf-ad6c-cd8b8ba6d206#0: "Exile target creature or planeswalker. You gain 2 life."

rows.question: cast Stomp off my bonecrusher giant, it resolved and went to exile. my opp says I can only cast the creature half from exile now, not Stomp again, is that right? also can they counter Stomp with a 'counter target creature spell' effect since the card is a creature?
rows.expected_answer: Your opponent is right. When an Adventure spell resolves it is exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and you may cast the card from exile — but only as the creature (Bonecrusher Giant), not as Stomp again (715.3d). And no, Stomp can't be hit by 'counter target creature spell': while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only its alternative characteristics (715.3a, 715.3b), so it is a red instant, not a creature spell. Everywhere else, including exile, the card is just the creature card Bonecrusher Giant (715.4).

outcome.answer:
Your opponent is right about the first part and wrong about the second. Once Stomp resolves, the card is exiled and you may cast only the creature half from there. Stomp is an Instant while it's a spell, so a "counter target creature spell" effect can't target it.

**Exile:** Per `715.3d`, the resolved Adventure is exiled, and "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can’t be cast as an Adventure this way." You can't cast Stomp again from exile. You can cast Bonecrusher Giant as a creature, and you must follow normal timing for that, which is usually main phase with an empty stack.

**Countering:** While Stomp is on the stack as an Adventure, `715.3b` says it "has only its alternative characteristics." Those are Stomp's, an instant Adventure with no creature type. Its normal characteristics as a creature card are ignored, so it isn't a creature spell. A Scryfall ruling agrees: the spell's characteristics are "determined by only those alternative characteristics." A "counter target creature spell" effect can't legally target it. A general counterspell, like one that says "counter target spell," still can. If Stomp is countered, it goes to the graveyard instead of exile, and you lose the option to cast the creature later.
citations: rule 715.3d: "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can’t be cast as an Adventure this way"
rule 715.3b: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."
ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/700df45a4e7078ff: "The spell's color, mana cost, mana value, and so on are determined by only those alternative characteristics."

rows.question: melded my Bruna and Gisela into Brisela and then it got Path to Exiled. does that count as one creature leaving or two for my [[Blood Artist]] type triggers, and do I get one Plains or two off Path?
rows.expected_answer:
Blood Artist does not trigger at all here: Path to Exile exiles Brisela, and Blood Artist
triggers on a creature dying, which means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield
(700.4). Exile is not dying. If Brisela instead died (say, to a Wrath of God), Blood Artist
would trigger exactly once: one permanent left the battlefield, even though the melded
permanent is a single object represented by two cards (712.21, 701.42a). A trigger reading
"whenever a card is put into a graveyard" would see two cards (712.21e). Either way, the
search happens once and Bruna and Gisela both go to exile. It is Brisela's controller who
searches, not the player who cast Path to Exile ("Its controller may search their library
for a basic land card"), and any basic land will do, not only a Plains.

rows.question: old school question. my Waylay (Urza's Saga printing) says 'at end of turn, remove them from the game'. so I cast it during my opponent's end step, the knights survive since the end step already started, and I get to swing with them on my turn right? classic waylay trick
rows.expected_answer: No — that trick was closed by errata. The printed text is not what the card does; you always use the current Oracle wording (108.1), which is 'Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step.' If you cast Waylay in your opponent's end step, the Knights are exiled at that same turn's cleanup step: the game checks for triggered abilities waiting during cleanup, puts the 'beginning of the next cleanup step' trigger on the stack, and then players get priority and another cleanup step follows (514.3a). You never get to attack with them. (Casting it during your opponent's declare-attackers step to get surprise blockers still works.)

outcome.answer:
No, the Knights won't survive to your turn. **Waylay**'s current Oracle text reads "Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step." It no longer says "at end of turn, remove them from the game", so that older wording doesn't apply.

Resolving Waylay creates a delayed triggered ability (`603.7`). It waits for the next cleanup step, which is the next step of that same turn, because "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup" (`512.1`). When the cleanup step begins, the game checks for triggered abilities waiting to go on the stack, "including those that trigger 'at the beginning of the next cleanup step'". The ability goes on the stack and resolves, and the Knights are exiled (`514.3a`). They never reach your turn.
citations: oracle f0db78c7-09b5-4981-8ca8-6dbab597c5d9#0: "Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step."
rule 603.7: "An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time."
rule 512.1: "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup."
rule 514.3a: "any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”)"

rows.question: my mirage LED says 'play this ability as an interrupt'. so it's a mana ability and I can crack it in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to pay for it right? that way I still have tutor as the last card when I discard
rows.expected_answer: No. Ignore the printed 'interrupt' text and use the current Oracle wording (108.1): 'Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant.' It is still a mana ability — the timing restriction doesn't change that (605.1) — but 'Activate only as an instant' means you may only activate it when you have priority (602.5e), so you can't activate it while paying for a spell the way 605.3a normally allows for mana abilities. The correct play is to cast Infernal Tutor with Tutor as the last card in hand, hold priority, then activate LED in response; when Tutor resolves you are hellbent and the mana is still floating.

outcome.answer:
No. LED is a mana ability, but you can't activate it while you're in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor. Your Mirage copy's "play this ability as an interrupt" is old wording. The current Oracle text is "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant." Interrupts no longer exist.

Being a mana ability doesn't remove the timing restriction. The rules say mana abilities keep "what timing restrictions (such as “Activate only as an instant”) they may have" (605.1). "Activate only as an instant" means you follow the timing rules for casting an instant (602.5e). An instant can be cast "any time they have priority" (117.1a), and you don't get priority until casting is finished (601.2i). So you can't crack LED to pay for Tutor.

The usual line is to pay for Tutor with other mana, cast it, and hold priority. Then activate LED in response. Tutor moved to the stack when you began casting it (601.2a), so it isn't in your hand for the discard either way. If your hand is empty when Tutor resolves, Hellbent applies and you can search for any card.
citations: oracle ee6099b0-fb1f-42f1-b862-7708c6e36d05#0: "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant."
rule 605.1: "what timing restrictions (such as “Activate only as an instant”) they may have"
rule 602.5e: "mean the player must follow the timing rules for casting an instant spell"
rule 117.1a: "A player may cast an instant spell any time they have priority."
rule 601.2i: "If the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority."
rule 601.2a: "a player first moves that card (or that copy of a card) from where it is to the stack."

rows.question: ok so I have [[Blood Artist]] out and my opponent wraths with [[Wrath of God]]. Blood Artist dies at the same time as everything else so does it even see the other creatures die? do I drain for all of them or just itself?
rows.expected_answer: Yes, you drain for every creature that died, including Blood Artist itself. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities 'look back in time' (603.10, 603.6c): the game checks the state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield, so it sees every creature that died simultaneously, including itself. All those triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3), and you choose a target player for each one.

outcome.answer:
Yes, you drain for all of them. **Blood Artist** sees every creature that dies at the same time as it, itself included. Each death triggers it separately, so it triggers once per creature.

Leaves-the-battlefield triggers "look back in time" (`603.10a`). The game checks the battlefield as it was immediately before **Wrath of God** destroyed everything, so Blood Artist's ability counts every creature that died, even though it left the battlefield at the same moment. The `603.10a` example is the same situation: an artifact with "Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life" triggers for each creature even though it goes to the graveyard at the same time as them. Scryfall's ruling on Blood Artist says the same: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."

Each trigger has you gain 1 life and makes a target player lose 1 life. Each one targets separately, so you can choose the same player for all of them or different players.
citations: rule 603.10a: "Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities"
rule 603.10a: "The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures."
ruling 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d/eaf0e0e76c3621ab: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."
oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

outcome.answer: Yes, you can cast a second **Lightning Bolt** before he gets to respond. Your buddy is right that he can't respond until you pass priority, but you aren't forced to pass. After you cast a spell, you get priority again (`117.3c`): "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward." You can cast the second Bolt on top of the first, and it will resolve first (`117.7`). Your opponent only gets priority once you pass (`117.3d`). The top object then resolves only if all players pass in succession (`117.4`). He can counter or respond to the whole stack at that point. If both Bolts target the same creature and the first one kills it, the second has no legal target and doesn't resolve (`608.2b`).
citations: rule 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward."
rule 117.3d: "If a player has priority and chooses not to take any actions, that player passes."
rule 117.4: "If all players pass in succession (that is, if all players pass without taking any actions in between passing), the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves"
rule 117.7: "The new spell or ability will resolve first."
rule 608.2b: "If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve."

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

outcome.answer:
No to both. Your creature doesn't die, and you can't respond between the second Ragavan arriving and the legend rule applying.

**Toughness 0 mid-resolution:** State-based actions are only checked when a player would get priority, and "state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability" (`704.4`). Nobody gets priority while a spell resolves (`117.2e`). If your creature's toughness is back above 0 when the other spell finishes resolving, the 0-toughness check (`704.5f`) never sees it. The **Maro** ruling says the same: it "won't be put into your graveyard when state-based actions are checked." Giant Growth resolves as its own spell, separately from the other one. Its +3/+3 ("Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn") only matters if it has already resolved when the check happens.

**Two Ragavan:** The legend rule is a state-based action (`704.5j`): the controller chooses one, and the rest go to the graveyard. State-based actions are performed "each time a player would get priority" (`117.5`) and "don't use the stack" (`704.1`). Nobody gets priority between the second Ragavan entering and the check, and there is nothing on the stack to respond to. You can only respond while the second Ragavan is still a spell on the stack, for example a dashed one. Once it has entered, the legend rule applies immediately.
citations: rule 704.4: "Unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability."
rule 117.2e: "Even if a player is doing so, no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving."
rule 704.5f: "If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard."
ruling ef32258a-d567-4fbc-ab85-8c00080f5b36/654c63e82671903c: "it won’t be put into your graveyard when state-based actions are checked."
oracle 5748ebf1-24e3-499d-ab7c-c2cebd462a24#0: "Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn."
rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards."
rule 117.5: "Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event"
rule 704.1: "State-based actions don’t use the stack."

rows.question: I attack with a 5/5 trample that also has deathtouch (Questing Beast) and they block with a 4/4. how much can I trample over? my opponent says I have to assign 4 to the blocker first
rows.expected_answer: The premise is off: Questing Beast is a 4/4 with vigilance, deathtouch and haste, and it does not have trample, so blocked by one creature it assigns all its combat damage to that blocker and nothing goes to the player (510.1c). A good answer says so. For the creature the asker describes, a 5/5 with trample and deathtouch, you only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 and can trample 4 over to the player. Trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blockers before excess goes to the player (702.19b), but any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that purpose (702.2c). Damage assignment for a blocked creature follows 510.1c, then all combat damage is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between (510.2). The 4/4 is then destroyed by deathtouch as an SBA.

outcome.answer: Your opponent is wrong: with deathtouch you only have to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 blocker, so you can trample over 4. One caveat: **Questing Beast**'s current Oracle text is "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste" and it has no trample. You'd need trample from another source, and I'm assuming that's where the 5/5 comes from. Under trample, per 702.19b, you must assign lethal damage to all blockers before assigning the excess to the player. Per 702.2c, "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt." So 1 damage to the blocker counts as lethal, and the other 4 can go to the defending player (or to the planeswalker you're attacking, if you attacked one). The 4/4 has enough power to block Questing Beast, since its evasion only stops blockers with power 2 or less.
citations: rule 702.2c: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt."

rule 702.19b: "Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as its controller chooses among those blocking creatures and the player, planeswalker, or battle the creature is attacking."
oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"

rows.question: commander q: my commander is [[Kenrith, the Returned King]]. two things: 1) can I run Nicol Bolas, the Ravager since Kenrith's text mentions all 5 colors? and 2) someone bounced Kenrith to my hand with Unsummon - does he go to the command zone or is that only for graveyard/exile?
rows.expected_answer: 1) Yes. Color identity includes mana symbols in the mana cost AND in the rules text (903.4), so Kenrith's identity is WUBRG even though his mana cost is only {4}{W}. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager (UBR) is legal because every color in its identity is in Kenrith's (903.5c). 2) Yes, Kenrith can go to the command zone. If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead - a replacement effect (903.9b). Graveyard/exile use a separate state-based action (903.9a). Either way it's optional.

outcome.answer:
1) Yes. **Kenrith, the Returned King** has {W} in his mana cost and {R}, {G}, {U} and {B} in his rules text, so his color identity is all five colors. Per 903.4, color identity is the color of "any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text". Per 903.5c, a card can be in your deck if every color in its identity is also in your commander's. **Nicol Bolas, the Ravager** is blue, black and red, so he fits. His back face is included in his color identity (903.4d), but it is also just blue, black and red.

2) It isn't only for the graveyard and exile. When **Unsummon** would put your commander into your hand, you may put him into the command zone instead (903.9b). This is a replacement effect and it's optional, so you can let him go to your hand if you'd rather recast him without commander tax. The state-based action in 903.9a is the separate rule that covers a commander already in a graveyard or exile.
citations: oracle d209b948-9afb-4fd1-a961-72c87282878c#0: "{4}{B}: Put target creature card from a graveyard onto the battlefield under its owner's control."
rule 903.4: "The color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text"
rule 903.5c: "A card can be included in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck’s commander."
rule 903.4d: "The back face of a double-faced card (see rule 712) is included when determining a card’s color identity."
rule 903.9b: "If a commander would be put into its owner’s hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead."
rule 903.9a: "If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone."

rows.question: commander damage question. I've been hit for 15 by my opponent's Rafiq. she then copies it with a Clone and hits me for 6 more with the clone. do I lose? also does the 21 count noncombat damage like from Fling?
rows.expected_answer: No to both. A player loses when they've been dealt 21 or more COMBAT damage by the SAME commander over the course of the game (903.10a; checked as a state-based action, 704.6c). The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 damage isn't commander damage - you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq. Fling damage is noncombat, so it never counts toward the 21 either; it just reduces your life total normally.

outcome.answer:
No, you don't lose to commander damage. Only the 15 from Rafiq counts toward the 21. The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 is a separate source. That assumes Rafiq is her designated commander. Noncombat damage such as Fling never counts toward the 21.

The loss condition is 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game." Being a commander is an attribute of the card, not of the object, and 903.3 says "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander." So the Clone's 6 adds nothing to the Rafiq total. Fling's damage doesn't count because 903.10a says "combat damage". Both the Clone's damage and Fling's damage still reduce your life total (119.2), so you can still lose normally if your life reaches 0 (119.6).
citations: rule 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."
rule 903.3: "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander."
rule 119.2: "Damage dealt to a player normally causes that player to lose that much life."
rule 119.6: "If a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game as a state-based action."

rows.question: two quick ones. 1) if I tap all my lands during my upkeep does that mana stick around so I can cast the mind sculptor in my main phase? 2) when I'm casting snappy can I tap lands in the middle of casting it or do I have to float the mana first?
rows.expected_answer: 1) No. Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana added during your upkeep is lost before your main phase (106.4). Tap the lands in your main phase instead. 2) Yes. Casting a spell includes a step where, if the total cost includes mana, you get a chance to activate mana abilities such as tapping lands (601.2g), and only then do you pay the total cost (601.2h). You do not need to float mana before announcing the spell.

outcome.answer: 1) No. Mana empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana you make in your upkeep is gone before your main phase. Tap the lands in your main phase, or while you cast **Jace, the Mind Sculptor**. 2) You don't need to float mana. Tap lands in the middle of casting **Snapcaster Mage**. Once the total cost is locked in, you get a chance to activate mana abilities, and that happens before you pay costs. Mana abilities don't use the stack, so you can activate them any time you're casting a spell and need to pay mana. Tapping a land for mana is a mana ability. Note that Snapcaster has flash, so you can cast it at instant speed. The same timing rules apply either way.
citations: rule 106.4: "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana."

rule 601.2g: "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."
rule 605.3a: "A player may activate an activated mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment"
rule 106.12: "To “tap [a permanent] for mana” is to activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes the {T} symbol in its activation cost."

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.

outcome.answer:
He loses 3 life for the Tim and 2 life for the Goyf. It isn't 5. ("Tim" is **Prodigal Sorcerer**, mana cost {2}{U}.)

**Dark Confidant** says "You lose life equal to its mana value." Per `202.3`, mana value is "the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color." Prodigal Sorcerer's {2}{U} gives mana value 3. **Tarmogoyf**'s {1}{G} gives mana value 2.

Goyf's power and toughness are set by its ability, "power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards". That doesn't change its mana cost, so a 5/6 Goyf still has mana value 2.
citations: oracle 2068185c-1b50-47d0-aa3f-bf505d199428#0: "You lose life equal to its mana value."
rule 202.3: "The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color."
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."
